# Visualizing Associations

## Scatter plots

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Appropriate for two continuous variables
- Each point is one observation
- Look for direction, strength, and shape of the relationship
- Example: head length vs. body mass in blue jays

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-blue-jays-scatter", fig_blue_jays_scatter(),
          w = 4.5, h = 3.4, x = 8.5, y = 2, width = 7)
```

## Bubble charts

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Map a third continuous variable to point size (here, skull size)
- Color or facets can add a categorical variable (here, sex)
- Differences in bubble size are hard to see

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-blue-jays-scatter-bubbles", fig_blue_jays_scatter_bubbles(),
          w = 6.5, h = 3.6, x = 8.3, y = 2, width = 7.4)
```

## Correlations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Correlation coefficient *r* ranges from -1 to 1
- Sign = direction; magnitude = strength
- *r* = 0 means no linear association
- Same *x* and *y* values in every panel, only the pairing changes

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-correlations", fig_correlations(),
          w = 6.4, h = 4.2, x = 8.5, y = 1.8, width = 7)
```

## Correlograms

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Summarize many pairwise correlations at once
- Color = direction and strength; circle size = magnitude
- Size de-emphasizes correlations near zero
- Pitfall: abstract, and hides the underlying data

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-forensic-correlations2", fig_forensic_correlations2(),
          w = 4, h = 4, x = 9, y = 1.4, width = 5.8)
```

## Summary of differences across groups

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Point = estimate; error bar = confidence interval
- Say what the bars represent (here, a 95% CI)
- Must select a reference group – here, chocolate from the US
- Dashed line at 0 = no difference from the reference group
- Could use aesthetics to highlight intervals that cross zero

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-confidence-visualizations-p2", fig_confidence_visualizations_p2(),
          w = 5.5, h = 3.5, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Using fitted lines to see associations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Confidence band: range of plausible fitted lines
- Confidence bands resemble alternative possible draws from the data
- Both show the same uncertainty in different ways
- Draws help avoid reading the band as exact

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-blue-jays-male-conf-band", fig_blue_jays_male_conf_band(),
          w = 5.5, h = 3.0, x = 8.8, y = 0.9, width = 6.4)
place_fig("fig-blue-jays-male-fitted-draws", fig_blue_jays_male_fitted_draws(),
          w = 5.5, h = 3.0, x = 8.8, y = 4.8, width = 6.4)
```

## Using fitted lines to see associations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Same data, four different fits
- Linear: simple but may miss curvature
- Quadratic and cubic: bend, but can behave oddly at the ends
- Spline: flexible; follows the data most closely
- Choice of model can increase complexity and highlight storytelling

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-fit-comparison", fig_fit_comparison(),
          w = 5.5, h = 4.4, x = 8.3, y = 1.4, width = 7)
```
